facts.text: White has exactly 20 legal first moves: sixteen pawn moves and four knight moves.
After White and Black have each made one move there are 400 different move sequences. After two moves each there are 197,281.
The 197,281 move sequences of two moves each lead to only 72,078 different positions, because many sequences end up in the same place.
Chess programmers test their move generators by counting every possible move sequence of a given length. From the starting position, five half-moves give exactly 4,865,609 sequences.

In 1950 Claude Shannon estimated that there are at least about 10^120 possible chess games. That is an estimate, not a count, and it is far more than the roughly 10^80 atoms thought to be in the observable universe.
Eight queens can be placed on a chessboard so that none attacks another in exactly 92 ways, or 12 ways if rotations and mirror images count as the same.
A knight can visit every square of the board exactly once and finish a move away from where it began. There are 26,534,728,821,064 such closed tours when the direction counts.
Bobby Fischer proposed Fischer Random Chess, also called Chess960, in 1996. It has 960 possible starting arrangements of the back-rank pieces.
A position published by Nenad Petrović in 1964 gives White 218 legal moves. No position with more is known.
A player can have up to nine queens at once: the original queen plus eight pawns that have each reached the far rank.
The fastest possible checkmate is the fool's mate: 1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#. Black mates on the fourth half-move of the game.
The scholar's mate ends a game in four moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Qh5 Nf6 4.Qxf7#. It works only if Black does not defend f7.
Sam Loyd found a way to reach stalemate after only ten moves, the shortest known stalemate. It starts 1.e3 a5 2.Qh5 Ra6.
En passant is the only capture in chess where the capturing piece does not land on the square of the piece it captures.
Castling is the only move in which a player moves two pieces at once: the king and a rook.
A pawn that reaches the far rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour. It cannot stay a pawn and it cannot become a king.
If the same position occurs three times, the player to move can claim a draw. If it occurs five times, the draw is automatic.
A player can claim a draw when fifty moves by each side pass with no pawn move and no capture. After seventy-five such moves the draw is automatic.
If the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, the game is a draw by stalemate, however much material the other side has.
King against king, king and bishop against king, and king and knight against king are drawn at once, because checkmate is impossible.
Two knights cannot force checkmate against a lone king. A mate is possible only if the defender helps.
A bishop stays on squares of one colour for the whole game. Each player starts with one bishop for each colour.
A knight changes the colour of its square with every move.
The board is set up so that each player has a light square at their right-hand corner. That makes a1 a dark square.
The usual piece values (pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9) are rules of thumb for teaching. They are not part of the rules of chess.
With perfect play, a king and queen can checkmate a lone king in at most 10 moves, and a king and rook in at most 16.
Chess grew out of chaturanga, a board game played in northern India by the 7th century.
The word checkmate comes from the Persian phrase shah mat, often translated as the king is helpless.
The word rook comes from the Persian rukh, meaning chariot. In the oldest forms of the game the piece really was a chariot, not a tower.
The bishop began as an elephant. Russian still calls it a slon, which means elephant, and French calls it a fou, meaning jester.
For centuries the queen could move only one square diagonally. She gained her modern long-range power in Spain in the 15th century, which made the game much faster.
The pawn's two-square first move was added in the Middle Ages, between the 13th and 16th centuries, to speed games up. En passant came with it or soon after.
The Lewis chessmen were found on the Isle of Lewis in Scotland in 1831. They were carved mostly from walrus ivory in the 12th century.
The Turk, a chess-playing machine shown from 1770, was a hoax. A skilled player hidden inside the cabinet moved the pieces.
Chess clocks were first used in competition at the London tournament of 1883. They were invented by Thomas Bright Wilson of the Manchester Chess Club.
The international chess federation, FIDE, was founded in Paris on 20 July 1924, on the closing day of an unofficial chess Olympiad.
The first official Chess Olympiad was held in London in 1927. The first Women's World Champion, Vera Menchik, won her title at the same event.
The International Olympic Committee recognised FIDE in 1999.
FIDE adopted the Elo rating system in 1970. It was devised by Arpad Elo, a chess master and physics professor.
FIDE created the grandmaster title in 1950 and gave it to 27 players that year.
The first official World Chess Championship match was played in 1886, when Wilhelm Steinitz beat Johannes Zukertort.
Emanuel Lasker was world champion from 1894 to 1921, 27 years, the longest reign of any champion.
Alexander Alekhine is the only world champion to have died while holding the title. He was champion again from 1937 until his death in 1946.
From Mikhail Botvinnik in 1948 to Boris Spassky in 1972, every world champion was from the Soviet Union. Bobby Fischer ended that run in Reykjavik in 1972.
The 1984-85 match between Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov was stopped without a winner after 48 games, when the FIDE president ended it. It is the only world championship match ever ended that way.
Garry Kasparov became the undisputed world champion in 1985, aged 22. Gukesh Dommaraju broke that record in 2024, winning the title aged 18.
Gukesh Dommaraju won the 2024 World Championship against Ding Liren by 7.5 to 6.5, deciding the match in the 14th and last game.
Magnus Carlsen reached a FIDE rating of 2882 in May 2014, the highest rating achieved since FIDE introduced the system in 1970.
Magnus Carlsen became a grandmaster at the age of 13.
Abhimanyu Mishra became the youngest grandmaster in history on 30 June 2021, aged 12 years, 4 months and 25 days. He beat the record Sergey Karjakin set in 2002 at 12 years and 7 months.
Judit Polgár became a grandmaster in 1991 at 15 years and 4 months, the youngest in history at that time.
In 2002 Judit Polgár beat Garry Kasparov, then the world number one, in a rapid game.
Judit Polgár's highest rating was 2735, in July 2005. She announced her retirement from competitive chess in 2014.
Vera Menchik won the first Women's World Championship in 1927. Male masters who lost to her were jokingly said to have joined the Vera Menchik Club.

In February 1996 Garry Kasparov beat the computer Deep Blue by 4 to 2 in Philadelphia, but Deep Blue won the first game, the first win by a computer over a reigning world champion in a game with tournament time controls.
In May 1997 Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by 3.5 to 2.5 in New York. Kasparov resigned the deciding sixth game after only 19 moves.
Stockfish, the chess engine inside this app, is free and open-source software. Anyone can read how it works and contribute improvements.
This app recognises more than 3,000 named openings and variations from a public-domain opening list. It matches them by position, so a transposition is still found.
Under the touch-move rule, a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if it has a legal move.
The two kings can never stand on neighbouring squares, because a king may not move to a square that the other king attacks.
In June 1970 the cosmonauts of Soyuz 9 played a game of chess against ground control while in orbit. It ended in a draw.
